issues.legal_issue: A custodian’s taking possession of property under the former local evacuee-property law did not require a prior inquiry and did not, for that reason alone, violate natural justice.
material_facts: The properties were taken into the Custodian’s possession under the local law because the owner had not returned to the State.
The local law provided for preservation and management of evacuee property and did not require an inquiry before the Custodian took possession.
issues.conclusion: The taking of possession was an administrative act under the local law, and the absence of a prior inquiry did not make it a violation of natural justice.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Junagadh State Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 1948, property of an evacuee vested in the Custodian and the Custodian was required to take possession of it; unlike the later central law, the local law did not provide for an inquiry before taking possession. The scheme preserved property pending its possible restoration and did not, in itself, offend natural justice.

predicates.custodian_property_takeover_under_local_: A custodian took possession of property under a local law governing evacuee property.
predicates.local_law_requires_no_pre_takeover_inqui: The local law did not require an inquiry before the custodian took possession of the property.
predicates.evacuee_property_preservation_proceeding: The proceeding concerned a custodian’s taking and preservation of property treated as evacuee property.

issues.definition: When a custodian takes possession under a local evacuee-property law that requires no prior inquiry, the takeover is not invalid merely because no such inquiry occurred.

issues.legal_issue: Property taken into custody as evacuee property under a repealed law could become validly vested evacuee property under the replacement law without a fresh declaration.
material_facts: The properties had been taken into the Custodian’s possession as evacuee properties under the local law before the central ordinance came into force.
They remained in the Custodian’s possession when the central ordinance and then the Act came into force.
The Act’s retrospective provision deemed property that purported to have vested under a repealed law to have validly vested and deemed it evacuee property under the Act.
issues.conclusion: The properties were evacuee property validly vested in the Custodian under the Act, and no fresh declaration under the later law was required.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 8(2) and 8(2A) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 deemed property vested under a repealed law to be evacuee property vested under the Act; subsection (2A), given retrospective effect, validated the vesting and related actions even where the earlier law or procedure was defective. The Court relied on The Dominion of India v. Shrinbai A. Irani, Azimunissa v. Deputy Custodian Evacuee Properties, and Haji Ismail Noor Mohammad and Co. v. Competent Officer, which recognized the validating and deeming effect of these provisions and the absence of a need for a fresh declaration.

predicates.property_claim_under_successor_evacuee_p: A claim concerns property dealt with under a successor law governing evacuee property.
predicates.property_taken_as_evacuee_property_under: A custodian had taken the property as evacuee property under a law that was later repealed.
predicates.property_remained_with_custodian_at_succ: The property was still in the custodian’s possession when the successor law came into force.

issues.definition: When property was taken as evacuee property under a repealed law and remained with the custodian when the successor law took effect, it is treated as validly vested evacuee property without a fresh declaration.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court cannot decide matters that the evacuee-property legislation assigns to the Custodian or determine the legality of actions taken under that legislation.
material_facts: The heirs brought a civil suit seeking possession of property and damages, alleging that the property was not evacuee property and challenging the Custodian’s actions and related administrative orders.

The governing Act barred civil courts from deciding whether property was evacuee property, questioning the legality of Custodian action, or deciding matters assigned to the Custodian or Custodian General.
The relevant administrative orders and the refusal to issue a restoration certificate were not challenged through the constitutional remedies identified by the Court.
issues.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to decide whether the properties were evacuee property or to review the challenged Custodian and Custodian General decisions; those unchallenged decisions had become final.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 28 and 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 made specified orders final and barred civil or revenue courts from deciding evacuee-property status, questioning the legality of Custodian action, or deciding matters entrusted to the Custodian or Custodian General. The bar did not displace the constitutional jurisdiction of the High Courts or Supreme Court. The Court relied on Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab v. Jafran Begum in applying the broad civil-court jurisdiction bar.

predicates.civil_suit_claiming_property_or_damages: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking property or damages.
predicates.suit_questions_evacuee_status_or_custodi: The suit asks the court to decide whether property is evacuee property or to question an action taken by a custodian under the governing scheme.
predicates.matter_assigned_to_evacuee_property_auth: The question is one that the governing scheme assigns to the custodian or another evacuee-property authority.

issues.definition: A civil court cannot decide a property or damages suit to the extent it asks the court to determine evacuee status or review a matter assigned to an evacuee-property authority.

issues.legal_issue: An alleged order restoring property under the former local law did not end the Custodian’s vesting unless the required governmental authorization was published in the official gazette.
material_facts: The heirs alleged that an order had directed the return of the properties to the owner.
The alleged order was not produced, and no official-gazette notification authorizing restoration was produced.
The properties remained in the Custodian’s possession after the alleged order.
issues.conclusion: Even if an order directing return had been made, it did not end the vesting under the local law without proof that the State Government had authorized restoration by a notification published in the official gazette.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 16(1) of the Junagadh State Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 1948, property taken as evacuee property continued to vest in the Custodian until the State Government authorized its restoration by notification in the official gazette. An unproduced or unpublished order did not establish that the statutory condition for restoration had been met.

predicates.custodian_property_claim: A claim concerns property held by a custodian as evacuee property under a local law.
predicates.property_vested_under_local_evacuee_law: The property had vested in the custodian under the local evacuee-property law.
predicates.claimed_restoration_order_lacks_required: A party relies on a purported restoration order, but the required official publication authorizing restoration is not established.

issues.definition: When property vested under a local evacuee-property law and the required official publication authorizing restoration is not established, the custodian’s vesting continues.

issues.legal_issue: Publication of a notification vesting property under the displaced-persons compensation scheme extinguished the former owner’s rights in that property.
material_facts: A notification under the displaced-persons compensation legislation was published in respect of the properties.
The former owner’s heirs later sought possession of those properties.
issues.conclusion: On publication of the notification, the former owner’s right, title, or interest in the properties was extinguished, and the properties vested absolutely in the Central Government free from encumbrances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 provided for property covered by a notification under section 12 to vest absolutely in the Central Government, free from encumbrances. The Court relied on Basant Ram v. Union of India.

predicates.civil_claim_for_property: A claimant brings a civil claim seeking property or an interest in it.
predicates.property_included_in_compensation_scheme: A notification under a compensation and rehabilitation scheme covers the property.

issues.definition: When a compensation-scheme vesting notification covers property, a civil claim based on the former owner’s interest cannot preserve that interest against the resulting absolute government vesting.
